q: A nurse records four observations about a patient. Which one is quantitative?
c: Heart rate is 88 beats per minute.
y: It is a number with a unit, so it is a measurement: a quantitative observation.
Warm and dry are descriptions in words with no number, so this is qualitative.
An odor described in words is qualitative; nothing was measured.
Cloudy is a quality you see, not a measured number with a unit, so it is qualitative.
h: Look for the observation that has both a number and a unit.
w: A quantitative observation is a measurement: a number with a unit. Only 88 beats per minute fits. The other three describe qualities (temperature feel, odor, appearance) in words, so they are qualitative.

q: A crop advisor in Kern County inspects an almond orchard. Which of her notes is a qualitative observation?
c: The hulls on the north rows are split and brown.
The trees in row 4 are 5.2 m tall.
The soil moisture sensor reads 18% water by volume.
The irrigation line pressure is 30 psi.
y: Split and brown describe the hulls in words, with no measured number, so this is qualitative.
5.2 m is a number with a unit, so this is a quantitative measurement.
18% by volume is a measured number from an instrument, so it is quantitative.
30 psi is a number with a unit (pounds per square inch), so it is quantitative.
h: Qualitative observations describe qualities in words; quantitative ones are numbers with units.
w: Only the note about split, brown hulls uses words instead of a measurement. Height, soil moisture and line pressure are all numbers with units, so they are quantitative.

q: A lab partner writes “the mass of the beaker was 12” in his notebook. What is the problem with this observation?
c: It has no unit, so the measurement is incomplete.
It is qualitative, so it cannot be recorded.
A mass can never be a whole number.
Masses must be written as words, not numbers.
y: A number without a unit does not say whether it was 12 g, 12 mg or 12 kg, so it is an incomplete measurement.
A number is not a qualitative observation; the issue is what is missing from the number.
Whole-number readings are possible; the issue is something else that is missing.
Measurements are written as numbers; words are for qualitative observations.
h: Could you tell from the note whether the beaker was very light or very heavy?
w: A quantitative observation needs a number and a unit. “12” alone could mean 12 g or 12 kg, so it is incomplete without a unit. Always write the unit, for example 12.4 g.

q: Which statement is a testable (falsifiable) hypothesis?
c: Watering tomato plants with 2 L of water per day instead of 1 L per day increases the mass of fruit they produce.
Tomato plants are happier when they are grown with love.
Some force that can never be detected decides how big tomatoes grow.
Tomatoes are the most beautiful plants in the garden.
y: It names something you can change (water per day) and something you can measure (fruit mass), so an experiment could show it is wrong.
“Happier” cannot be measured, so no experiment could prove this wrong.
A force that can never be detected can never be tested, so this cannot be falsified.
Beauty is an opinion, not something an experiment can measure or disprove.
h: A falsifiable hypothesis is one an experiment could prove wrong. Which one names something you can change and something you can measure?
w: A scientific hypothesis must be testable: an experiment must be able to show it is wrong. The watering statement has a variable you change (water per day) and a result you measure (fruit mass). Happiness, undetectable forces and beauty cannot be measured, so those statements cannot be tested.

q: A microbiology student incubates identical agar plates, each spread with the same sample of E. coli, at 25 °C, 30 °C and 37 °C. After 24 hours she counts the colonies on each plate. What is the independent variable?
c: The number of colonies on each plate
The type of agar in the plates
y: Temperature is the one thing she changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable.
The colony count is what she measured; it depends on the change she made.
Every plate was incubated for 24 hours, so time was kept constant.
All the plates used the same agar, so it was kept constant.
h: Ask: what did she deliberately change from plate to plate?
w: The independent variable is the one thing the experimenter deliberately changes: the incubation temperature. The colony count is the dependent variable (what she measured), and the time and agar type are constants kept the same for every plate.

q: A respiratory therapy student fills identical humidifier chambers with water heated to 30 °C, 35 °C or 40 °C and measures how much water evaporates from each in 1 hour. What is the dependent variable?
c: The mass of water that evaporates in 1 hour
The size of the humidifier chamber
y: The amount of water evaporated is what he measures, and it depends on the temperature he set.
Temperature is what he changes on purpose, so it is the independent variable.
The chambers are identical, so chamber size is a constant.
Every trial lasts 1 hour, so time is a constant.
h: The dependent variable is the result you measure at the end.
w: The dependent variable is the measured result: the mass of water that evaporates. Water temperature is the independent variable he chooses, and the chamber size and 1-hour time are kept constant so the comparison is fair.

q: A Tulare County farmer wants to know whether a new compost increases pistachio yield. Which setup gives her a proper control?
c: A matching block of trees that gets no compost but the same water, soil and care
A block of trees that gets twice as much of the new compost
A block of trees in a different county with different soil and water
Weighing the nuts from the composted trees twice
y: The control is the trial without the change, with everything else kept the same, so any difference can be blamed on the compost.
This changes the amount of compost, which is a second test condition, not a comparison without the change.
Changing the soil and water too means she could not tell which difference caused a change in yield.
Repeating a measurement checks the measurement but gives nothing to compare against.
h: A control is the trial where you leave out the one change you are testing.
w: A fair experiment compares a trial with the change to a trial without it, keeping everything else the same. A matching block with no compost is the control. A block in a different county changes several things at once, so the result could not be traced to the compost.

q: Which statement is a scientific law?
c: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
Matter is made of atoms that are rearranged, but not created or destroyed, in reactions.
Adding more baking soda to this vinegar will make more bubbles.
The solution in flask 3 turned pink.
y: It describes what always happens without explaining why, which is what a law does (the law of conservation of mass).
This explains why mass is conserved using a model of atoms, so it is a theory.
This is a single untested prediction about one situation, so it is a hypothesis.
This is one qualitative observation, not a general statement about what always happens.
h: A law describes what always happens; a theory explains why.
w: A scientific law summarizes what always happens, often as an equation, without explaining why. Mass of products equals mass of reactants is the law of conservation of mass. The atom statement is the theory that explains it, the baking-soda prediction is a hypothesis, and the pink solution is an observation.

q: Which statement about a scientific theory is correct?
c: It is a well-tested explanation of why something happens, and it can be revised if new evidence demands it.
It becomes a law once enough experiments prove it.
It is a guess that has not been tested yet.
It describes what happens but never explains why.
y: A theory explains why, is backed by many experiments, and can still change with new evidence.
Theories and laws do different jobs (why versus what); a theory never graduates into a law.
That describes the everyday meaning of “theory”; in science an untested idea is a hypothesis.
Describing what happens without saying why is the job of a law.
h: In science, which is stronger: a guess or an explanation supported by many experiments?
w: In science a theory is a well-tested explanation of why nature behaves as it does, supported by many experiments, and it can be revised by new evidence (as models of the atom were). It does not turn into a law, and it is not a guess.

q: A student notices that cut apples turn brown, wonders why, and guesses that oxygen in air causes it. What should she do next in the scientific method?
c: Test the idea by leaving some apple slices in air and sealing others away from air
Declare that oxygen causes browning as a scientific law
Change her guess to a different idea before testing it
Stop, because she already has an explanation
y: After forming a hypothesis, the next step is an experiment that changes one thing (exposure to air) and measures the result.
One untested guess is not a law; a law comes only after results are repeated many times.
There is no reason to change a hypothesis before it has been tested.
An untested hypothesis is not yet supported by evidence; it still has to be tested.
h: Her guess is a hypothesis. What step comes right after forming a hypothesis?
w: She has observed, asked a question and formed a hypothesis. The next step is to experiment: compare slices exposed to air with slices sealed away from air, keeping everything else the same, then analyze the results.

q: A researcher's data do not support her hypothesis. What is the best next step?
c: Revise the hypothesis and test it again
Change the data so they fit the hypothesis
Repeat the same conclusion in a report
y: The scientific method is a cycle: results that do not support a hypothesis send you back to revise it and test again.
Changing data is dishonest and defeats the purpose of testing.
A theory must be supported by many experiments; this hypothesis was just contradicted.
Reporting a conclusion the data do not support would be inaccurate.
h: Think of the scientific method as a cycle rather than a straight line.
w: When data contradict a hypothesis, the scientist revises the hypothesis and tests again. This is how the cycle of the scientific method moves toward better explanations.

q: Classify the substance shown in the box.
c: An element made of diatomic molecules
A mixture of an element and a compound
y: Every particle is the same, and each contains only nitrogen atoms, so this is the element nitrogen in its N<sub>2</sub> form.
A compound needs two or more different elements bonded together; every atom here is the same kind.
Every particle in the box is identical, so there is only one substance, not a mixture.
There is only one kind of particle, and none of them contains two different elements.
h: First ask: is every particle the same? Then ask: how many kinds of atoms are in each particle?
w: All the particles are identical N2 molecules, so it is a pure substance. Each molecule has only one kind of atom, so it is an element. Nitrogen is one of the seven elements that exist as diatomic (two-atom) molecules; the subscript 2 does not make it a compound.

q: The box models a sample of water with some oxygen gas dissolved in it. How is the sample classified?
c: A mixture of an element and a compound
y: There are two kinds of particles: H<sub>2</sub>O (a compound of H and O) and O<sub>2</sub> (an element, only O atoms).
A pure substance has only one kind of particle; this box has two.
O<sub>2</sub> contains only one kind of atom, so it is an element, not a compound.
Some particles contain two different kinds of atoms bonded together, so the sample is not just an element.
h: Identify each kind of particle separately: does it contain one kind of atom or two?
w: The box holds two kinds of particles that are not bonded to each other, so it is a mixture. H2O molecules contain two elements (a compound) and O2 molecules contain one (an element): a mixture of an element and a compound. Every particle contains oxygen, but that does not make them the same substance.

q: Which box shows a pure compound?
y: Every particle in B is the same CO<sub>2</sub> molecule, made of two different elements bonded together.
A contains only one kind of atom, so it is an element, not a compound.
C contains two kinds of particles, each made of only one kind of atom: a mixture of elements.
D contains two different kinds of molecules, so it is a mixture, not a pure substance.
h: A pure compound has one kind of particle, and that particle contains two or more different kinds of atoms.
w: Box B has only CO2 molecules, each with C and O bonded together, so it is a pure compound. A is the element helium, C is a mixture of two elements (N2 and O2, a model of air), and D is a mixture of two compounds (CO2 and H2O).

q: Which box shows a mixture of an element and a compound?
y: B contains Cl<sub>2</sub> (one kind of atom, an element) mixed with HCl (two elements bonded, a compound).
A has only one kind of particle, so it is a pure substance (the compound water).
Both kinds of particles in C (NH<sub>3</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O) contain two different elements, so C is a mixture of two compounds.
Both kinds of particles in D are single atoms of one element each, so D is a mixture of two elements.
h: Check each kind of particle in a box: one kind of atom means element; two or more kinds bonded together means compound.
w: Box B mixes Cl2 molecules (an element) with HCl molecules (a compound). A is pure water, C is a mixture of two compounds (NH3 and H2O), and D is a mixture of two elements (helium and argon atoms).

q: Air high in the atmosphere contains both O<sub>2</sub> and ozone, O<sub>3</sub>. The box models such a sample. How is it classified?
c: A mixture of an element and a compound
y: O<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>3</sub> are different substances, but each contains only oxygen atoms, so this is a mixture of two forms of an element.
A compound needs two or more different elements; every atom here is oxygen.
A pure substance has one kind of particle; this box has two different molecules.
Neither particle contains a second element, so neither one is a compound.
h: Are all the particles identical? Does any particle contain more than one kind of atom?
w: The box has two different kinds of particles (O2 and O3) that are not bonded to each other, so it is a mixture. Each particle contains only oxygen atoms, so both are forms of the element oxygen: a mixture of two elements.

q: Which substance is an element?
y: O<sub>3</sub> has only one element symbol, so it is a form of the element oxygen even though it has a subscript.
C and O are two different elements bonded together, so CO is a compound.
H and O are two different elements bonded in a fixed ratio, so this is a compound.
Na and Cl are two different elements, so NaCl is a compound.
h: Count the different element symbols in each formula, not the subscripts.
w: A formula with only one element symbol is an element, subscript or not, so O3 is an element. CO, H2O2 and NaCl each contain two different elements bonded together, so they are compounds.

q: Which item is a homogeneous mixture?
c: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl dissolved in water)
y: Saline has salt dissolved evenly in water: uniform throughout, but its composition could be changed.
Blood looks uniform, but a microscope shows cells floating in plasma, so it is heterogeneous.
Distilled water is one substance, H<sub>2</sub>O, so it is a compound, not a mixture.
Pure iron contains only Fe atoms, so it is an element.
h: A homogeneous mixture contains more than one substance but looks the same everywhere, even under a microscope.
w: Normal saline is salt dissolved evenly in water: two substances, uniform throughout, so it is a homogeneous mixture (a solution). Whole blood is heterogeneous (cells in plasma), distilled water is a compound, and pure iron is an element.

q: A phlebotomist draws a tube of whole blood. Under a microscope, red cells, white cells and platelets float in a yellowish liquid. How is whole blood classified?
y: The microscope shows regions that differ (cells and liquid), so the mixture is not uniform: heterogeneous.
A homogeneous mixture looks the same everywhere, even under a microscope; blood does not.
Blood contains many substances physically mixed, with no fixed composition, so it is not a compound.
Blood contains many kinds of atoms and substances, so it is not an element.
h: Does blood look the same everywhere when you look closely enough?
w: Blood looks uniform to the eye, but the microscope shows cells suspended in plasma, and spinning it separates layers. That makes whole blood a heterogeneous mixture. (Plasma by itself, water with dissolved salts, glucose and proteins, is a homogeneous mixture.)

q: Which element does not exist as diatomic molecules under normal conditions?
y: Neon is a noble gas whose atoms stay single; it is not one of the diatomic seven.
Bromine is one of the diatomic seven (Br<sub>2</sub>), in the halogen column.
Hydrogen is one of the diatomic seven (H<sub>2</sub>), sitting alone at the top left.
Nitrogen is one of the diatomic seven (N<sub>2</sub>), at the start of the “7” shape.
h: The diatomic seven are H, N, O, F, Cl, Br and I.
w: The seven diatomic elements are H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2. Neon is not on that list; its atoms exist singly.

q: A clinical lab needs to separate the plasma from the blood cells in a blood sample quickly. Which method uses the difference in density between the parts?
y: Spinning the tube forces the denser cells to the bottom and leaves plasma on top, using differences in density.
Distillation uses differences in boiling point and would boil and damage the sample.
Filtration separates by particle size, and a coffee filter would not separate cells from plasma well.
Evaporation drives off the liquid, which would destroy the plasma rather than collect it.
h: Which method spins a sample so the denser parts settle?
w: Centrifugation spins the tube so the denser red blood cells pack at the bottom and the less dense plasma rises to the top. Separation methods work because the parts of a mixture are not bonded; each method uses a physical property (here, density).

q: Which method would best separate ethanol from water in a mixture of the two liquids?
y: Ethanol and water boil at different temperatures, so the one that boils first can be collected as vapor and condensed.
Filtration separates a solid from a liquid by particle size; both of these are dissolved liquids that pass through.
Decanting needs separate layers, but ethanol and water mix completely.
Neither ethanol nor water is attracted to a magnet.
h: The two liquids mix completely. What property differs between them?
w: Ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) and water (100 °C) form a homogeneous mixture, so you cannot filter or pour them apart. Distillation uses the difference in boiling point: ethanol vaporizes first and is condensed and collected.

q: Which state of matter has both a definite shape and a definite volume?
y: Solid particles are packed and vibrate in place, so a solid keeps its own shape and volume.
A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.
A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume; it fills its container.
Neither liquids nor gases keep their own shape.
h: Which state keeps its shape when you move it to a new container?
w: Only a solid has a definite shape and a definite volume, because its particles are packed closely and can only vibrate in place. Liquids keep their volume but not their shape; gases keep neither.

q: A 75 mL sample is poured from a beaker into a 250 mL flask. It settles into the bottom of the flask, still occupies 75 mL, and takes the flask's shape. What state is it in?
y: Its volume stayed the same but its shape changed to fit the container: definite volume, no definite shape.
A solid would keep its own shape instead of taking the flask's shape.
A gas would expand to fill all 250 mL of the flask.
The two clues (volume kept, shape changed) are enough to name the state.
h: Check two things: did the volume change, and did the shape change?
w: The sample kept its volume (75 mL) but took the shape of the flask. That is a liquid: its particles touch, so the volume stays fixed, but they slide past one another, so it flows. A gas would have filled the whole 250 mL flask.

q: Which description fits the particles of a gas?
c: Far apart, moving fast and randomly until they collide
Touching, and sliding past one another
Packed closely and vibrating in fixed positions
Touching and not moving at all
y: Gas particles are far apart with mostly empty space between them, and they move fast in straight lines between collisions.
Touching particles that slide past each other describe a liquid.
Closely packed particles vibrating in place describe a solid.
Particles are always moving; even in a solid they vibrate.
h: Describe two things: how far apart the particles are, and how they move.
w: In a gas the particles are far apart and move fast and randomly until they hit each other or the container walls. Liquid particles touch but slide past each other; solid particles are packed and vibrate in place.

q: Which statement about the particles in a solid, such as a piece of ice, is correct?
c: They do not move at all.
They are far apart from one another.
They slide freely past one another.
y: Solid particles are held in place by their neighbors but still vibrate back and forth.
A common mistake: solid particles do move; they vibrate in place.
Solid particles are packed closely together, not far apart.
Sliding past one another describes a liquid, which is why liquids flow.
h: Solid particles are not frozen in time. What kind of motion can they still have?
w: The particles in a solid are packed closely and held in position, but they vibrate in place. They do not stop moving, and they do not slide past each other (that is a liquid).

q: A respiratory therapist notes that a small steel cylinder holds hundreds of liters of oxygen gas at room pressure. Using the particle view, why can a gas be squeezed into such a small tank?
c: Gas particles are far apart, so most of a gas's volume is empty space that can be removed.
Gas particles shrink when they are put under pressure.
Gas particles touch one another, so they can be stacked more neatly.
Some of the gas particles are destroyed when the gas is compressed.
y: Pushing gas particles closer together only removes empty space, so the gas compresses easily.
The particles themselves keep their size; it is the space between them that shrinks.
Gas particles do not touch; touching particles (liquids and solids) barely compress.
Compressing a gas does not destroy any particles; the same particles just sit closer together.
h: Think about what is between the particles of a gas.
w: Gas particles are far apart, so a gas is mostly empty space. Compressing it pushes the particles closer together and removes some of that space, which is why a gas is easily compressible. The particles do not shrink or disappear.

q: One sealed syringe holds 20 mL of air and another holds 20 mL of water. You push hard on each plunger. What happens?
c: The air compresses noticeably; the water barely compresses.
Both compress by about the same amount.
The water compresses noticeably; the air barely compresses.
y: Air is a gas with lots of empty space between particles; water's particles already touch, leaving little space to remove.
Liquids and gases compress very differently because their particle spacing is so different.
This is reversed: liquid particles touch, so a liquid barely compresses.
Gases do compress, because their particles are far apart.
h: Compare how much empty space is between the particles in a gas and in a liquid.
w: The air compresses; the water barely does. Gas particles are far apart, so pushing removes empty space. Liquid particles already touch, so there is almost no space to remove.

q: Which of these solids is amorphous rather than crystalline?
y: Glass particles are jumbled with no regular repeating pattern, which makes it amorphous.
Salt is made of ions in a regular repeating pattern, so it is crystalline.
Water molecules in ice sit in a regular repeating pattern, so ice is crystalline.
Quartz has a regular repeating arrangement of atoms, so it is crystalline.
h: Crystalline solids have particles in a regular, repeating pattern. Which one has jumbled particles?
w: Glass is an amorphous solid: it holds its shape, but its particles are disordered. Table salt, ice and quartz are crystalline, with particles arranged in regular, repeating patterns.

q: Tooth enamel is built around hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate mineral whose particles sit in a regular, repeating pattern. How is enamel best described?
y: Particles in a regular, repeating pattern are what make a solid crystalline.
Amorphous solids have jumbled particles, not a regular repeating pattern.
Enamel keeps its shape under the force of chewing, which a liquid cannot do.
A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume; enamel has both.
h: The question tells you how the particles are arranged. Which kind of solid has a repeating pattern?
w: Enamel keeps a definite shape and volume, so it is a solid, and its mineral particles repeat in a regular pattern, so it is a crystalline solid. That ordered packing is part of why enamel is the hardest tissue in the body.

q: Which statement correctly describes the particles in a liquid?
c: They touch one another but are not held in fixed positions.
They are far apart with mostly empty space between them.
They are locked in fixed positions in a regular pattern.
They are spread evenly through the whole container.
y: Liquid particles are close enough to touch (so the volume stays fixed) but free to slide past each other (so it flows).
A common mistake: far-apart particles describe a gas, not a liquid.
Fixed positions in a regular pattern describe a crystalline solid.
Spreading through the whole container is what gas particles do.
h: Liquids barely compress. What does that tell you about the space between their particles?
w: Liquid particles touch but can move past one another. Because they touch, a liquid barely compresses and has a definite volume; because they slide, it flows and takes the shape of its container.

q: In the lungs, oxygen spreads out to fill each alveolus (a tiny air sac) completely. Which property of gases does this show?
c: A gas has no definite volume; it expands to fill its container.
A gas has a definite shape.
A gas has a definite volume but no definite shape.
A gas cannot move from one place to another.
y: Gas particles are far apart and move freely, so a gas spreads to fill whatever space it is in.
Gases have no shape of their own; they take the shape of the space they fill.
A definite volume with no definite shape describes a liquid.
Gas particles move fast, which is why gases spread out and move in and out of the lungs.
h: Does a gas keep its own volume, or does it fill the space it is in?
w: A gas has no definite volume or shape: its fast, far-apart particles spread to fill the entire container, here each alveolus. A liquid would only fill the bottom of the space it occupies.

q: A sodium ion, Na<sup>+</sup>, and a chloride ion, Cl<sup>−</sup>, are near each other. What happens?
c: They attract only if they touch.
y: One is positive and one is negative, and opposite charges attract.
Repulsion happens between like charges (+ and +, or − and −).
Both particles are charged, so there is a force between them.
The force acts across a distance; it gets stronger as they come closer, but it does not need contact.
h: Compare the signs of the two charges.
w: Na+ is positive and Cl− is negative. Opposite charges attract, and this attraction is what holds table salt together.

q: A calcium ion, Ca<sup>2+</sup>, and a sodium ion, Na<sup>+</sup>, are near each other. What happens?
c: They repel, because both are positive.
They attract, because Ca<sup>2+</sup> is more positive than Na<sup>+</sup>.
They attract, because their charges have different sizes.
y: Only the signs decide the direction; two positive charges always repel.
A common mistake: being “more positive” does not make two positive charges attract.
The size of the charges affects how strong the force is, not whether it attracts or repels.
Both ions are charged, so there is a force between them.
h: Direction (attract or repel) depends only on the signs, not the sizes, of the charges.
w: Both ions are positive, and like charges repel. The sizes (2+ and 1+) change how strong the push is, not its direction.

q: Four pairs of ions are each held the same distance apart. Which pair attracts most strongly?
y: At the same distance, the pair with the largest opposite charges (2+ and 2−) attracts most strongly.
These are opposite charges, but only 1+ and 1−, smaller than another pair's.
These attract, but with charges of only 1+ and 1−.
Both ions are positive, so this pair repels rather than attracts.
h: The distance is the same for every pair, so compare the sizes of the charges, and make sure the pair really attracts.
w: At the same distance, larger charges give a stronger force. Mg2+ and O2− have charges of 2+ and 2−, so they attract more strongly than the 1+/1− pairs. Ca2+ and Mg2+ are both positive, so they repel.

q: A K<sup>+</sup> ion and an F<sup>−</sup> ion move from 4 nm apart to 1 nm apart. How does the force between them change?
c: The force changes from attraction to repulsion.
y: The force between charges strengthens as the charges come closer together.
The force weakens as charges move apart, not as they move closer.
Distance matters: the same two charges attract more strongly when they are closer.
The signs did not change (still + and −), so they still attract.
h: The charges did not change. What did change, and which way does that push the strength of the force?
w: The charges stay 1+ and 1−, so they still attract, but the distance shrank. Charges pull on each other more strongly when they are closer, so the attraction gets stronger.

q: What must happen to pull a Na<sup>+</sup> ion and a Cl<sup>−</sup> ion farther apart?
c: Energy must be added, because the opposite charges attract each other.
Energy is released, because the ions want to separate.
No energy is involved, because the ions are neutral.
Energy is released, because like charges repel.
y: Opposite charges attract, so pulling them apart works against that attraction and takes energy.
Opposite charges pull toward each other; separating them costs energy rather than releasing it.
The ions are charged (+ and −), not neutral.
Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> have opposite charges, not like charges.
h: Think of pulling two magnets apart that are stuck together.
w: Because opposite charges attract, separating them is like pulling two magnets apart: energy must be added. When opposite charges come together, energy is released. This is why breaking up an ionic solid takes energy.

q: Two protons (each with a 1+ charge) are pushed closer and closer together. Which statement is correct?
c: The repulsion grows stronger, and pushing them together takes energy.
The protons begin to attract once they are close enough.
The repulsion gets weaker as they come closer.
y: Like charges repel, the force grows as the distance shrinks, and forcing like charges together takes energy.
Two positive charges repel at every distance in this model; they never start attracting.
Electric forces get stronger, not weaker, as the charges move closer.
Energy is released when opposite charges come together, not like charges.
h: First decide attract or repel from the signs; then think about what closer distance does to the force.
w: Two positive charges repel, and the push gets stronger as they get closer. Forcing like charges together works against that push, so it takes energy. (Energy is released only when opposite charges come together.)

q: An atom has 11 protons (each 1+) and 11 electrons (each 1−). What is its overall charge?
y: Equal amounts of positive and negative charge cancel, so the net charge is zero.
This counts the protons but forgets the 11 electrons that cancel them.
This counts the electrons but forgets the 11 protons that cancel them.
Electrons carry negative charge, so they subtract from the protons instead of adding.
h: Add the positive charges and the negative charges together.
w: 11 positive charges and 11 negative charges add to (+11) + (−11) = 0, so the atom is electrically neutral. An atom becomes an ion only when it gains or loses electrons.

q: On a dry winter day in Fresno, you rub a balloon on your hair. Electrons move from your hair onto the balloon, and the balloon then clings to your hair. Why?
c: The balloon becomes negative, your hair becomes positive, and opposite charges attract.
Both become negative, and like charges attract.
Both become positive, and like charges attract.
The balloon becomes positive because it gained electrons.
y: Gaining electrons makes the balloon negative; losing them leaves the hair positive; + and − attract.
Like charges repel, and the hair lost electrons, so it cannot become negative.
Like charges repel, and the balloon gained electrons, so it cannot become positive.
Electrons are negative, so gaining them makes an object negative, not positive.
h: Electrons are negative. Which object gained them, and which object lost them?
w: The balloon gains negative electrons and becomes negative; your hair loses them and is left positive. Opposite charges attract, so the balloon clings to your hair.

q: In a resting nerve cell, the inside of the membrane is slightly negative compared with the outside. When sodium channels open, Na<sup>+</sup> ions rush into the cell. Which idea best explains why?
c: Positive Na<sup>+</sup> ions are attracted to the negative interior.
Positive Na<sup>+</sup> ions are repelled by the negative interior.
Na<sup>+</sup> ions are neutral, so charge plays no role.
Like charges attract, so Na<sup>+</sup> moves toward other positive ions.
y: Opposite charges attract, so the positive ions are pulled toward the negative inside of the cell.
Repulsion happens between like charges; + and − attract.
Na<sup>+</sup> carries a 1+ charge; the plus sign shows it is an ion, not neutral.
Like charges repel; they do not attract.
h: Compare the charge of Na<sup>+</sup> with the charge on the inside of the cell.
w: The Na+ ions are positive and the cell interior is negative, so opposite charges attract and pull the ions inward. Keeping the charges separated beforehand costs the cell energy, which it spends running ion pumps.

q: Inside an X-ray tube, electrons released from a heated filament (the cathode) speed toward a target (the anode). What charge must the anode have to pull the electrons toward it?
c: Neutral, because electrons need no force to move
Negative, so it can repel the electrons forward
y: Electrons are negative, so a positive anode attracts them and speeds them up.
Like charges repel; a negative anode would push the electrons away from it.
The electrons speed up because a force acts on them; a neutral target would not pull them.
A negative anode would repel the electrons back toward the cathode, not draw them to the target.
h: What sign do electrons have, and what sign would pull them toward the target?
w: Electrons carry negative charge. A positive anode attracts them, and the large voltage across the tube makes that attraction strong, so the electrons strike the anode with enough energy to produce X-rays.

q: Which statement describes a chemical property of iron?
c: Iron is attracted to a magnet.
y: Rusting turns iron into a new substance (iron oxide), so the tendency to rust is a chemical property.
Melting point is measured without changing iron into a new substance, so it is a physical property.
Color and luster can be observed without changing the iron, so they are physical properties.
Being attracted to a magnet does not change the iron into anything new, so it is a physical property.
h: A chemical property describes how a substance can turn into a different substance.
w: A chemical property can only be observed by trying a change that forms a new substance. Iron rusting forms iron oxide, so it is a chemical property. Melting point, color and magnetism are observed without changing iron's identity, so they are physical properties.

q: Which of these is a chemical change?
c: An egg white turns solid and white as it cooks
An ice cube melts on a tray
A tablet is split in half
y: Cooking changes the proteins in egg white into new forms that do not change back when cooled, so new substances form.
Melting only changes the state; the water molecules are still H<sub>2</sub>O.
Dissolving is physical; evaporating the coffee's water would give the sugar back.
Splitting a tablet changes its size, not what it is made of.
h: Ask: is it still the same stuff afterward, and could you get the original back just by cooling, drying or picking pieces apart?
w: Cooking an egg is a chemical change: the proteins are changed into new forms with different properties, and cooling does not undo it. Melting, dissolving and splitting change form or state but not the identity of the substance.

q: A pot of water is heated on a stove and bubbles form throughout the liquid. What kind of change is this, and why?
c: Physical, because the bubbles are water vapor and no new substance forms
Chemical, because bubbles always mean a new gas formed
Physical, because the water breaks into hydrogen and oxygen gas
y: The bubbles in boiling water are H<sub>2</sub>O in the gas state; only the state changed.
Bubbles are a clue, not proof; boiling makes bubbles without forming a new substance.
Supplying heat does not by itself make a change chemical; many physical changes need heat.
If water broke into hydrogen and oxygen, that would be a chemical change, and boiling does not do that.
h: What gas is inside the bubbles of boiling water?
w: Boiling is vaporization, a physical change: the bubbles are water vapor, still H2O. Bubbles signal a chemical change only when they form without boiling (for example, peroxide foaming on a wound).

q: A nurse takes a cold IV bag out of the medication refrigerator, and water droplets form on the outside of the bag. What is the name of this change of state?
y: Water vapor in the room air cools on the cold bag and turns from a gas into liquid droplets.
Evaporation is liquid turning into gas, the reverse of what forms the droplets.
Deposition is gas turning directly into a solid, like frost; these droplets are liquid.
Melting is a solid turning into a liquid; nothing solid was involved here.
h: The droplets came from water vapor in the air. Which change goes from gas to liquid?
w: Water vapor in the air touches the cold bag, cools, and becomes liquid droplets: condensation (gas → liquid). Like every change of state, it is a physical change; the molecules are still H2O.

q: On winter mornings, tule fog forms in the Central Valley when water vapor near the cold ground turns into tiny liquid droplets that hang in the air. How is the formation of tule fog classified?
y: Gas becoming liquid is condensation, and the water molecules do not change, so it is physical.
The name is right, but changes of state are physical changes; no new substance forms.
Sublimation goes from solid directly to gas; fog forms from gas becoming liquid.
Vaporization goes from liquid to gas, and changes of state are never chemical changes.
h: Name the starting and ending states, then ask whether any new substance formed.
w: Water vapor (gas) becomes liquid droplets: condensation, a physical change. When the sun warms the air, the droplets evaporate and the fog lifts; the water molecules never change, only their state.

q: In the catalase test, a microbiology student adds a drop of hydrogen peroxide to a bit of a bacterial colony and the drop bubbles vigorously as oxygen gas forms. What does the bubbling show?
c: A chemical change: peroxide is broken down into new substances, water and oxygen
A physical change: the peroxide is boiling
A physical change: the peroxide is evaporating
A physical change: oxygen was already dissolved and is escaping
y: A new gas forms without heating because H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is broken into new substances, water and O<sub>2</sub>.
Nothing was heated, and the gas is oxygen, a new substance, not peroxide vapor.
Evaporation would not make vigorous bubbles of a new gas, oxygen.
The oxygen is produced as the enzyme catalase breaks down peroxide; it was not simply dissolved there before.
h: Gas forming without boiling is one of the signs of a chemical change. What new substances form?
w: The bacterium's enzyme, catalase, breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. New substances form, so the bubbling is a chemical change. Catalase-positive bacteria, such as Staphylococcus, bubble; bacteria without catalase do not.

q: Which of these properties of a silver ring is extensive?
y: Volume depends on how much silver there is, so it is extensive.
Melting point is the same for a speck or a bar of silver, so it is intensive.
Color does not depend on the amount of silver, so it is intensive.
Density is mass divided by volume, which stays the same for any amount, so it is intensive.
h: An extensive property changes if you have more or less of the sample.
w: Extensive properties depend on the amount of sample: volume (and mass) would double for a ring twice as large. Melting point, color and density are intensive; they are the same for any amount, which makes them useful for identifying a substance.

q: A lab note reads: “The acetone spilled on the bench evaporated within a few minutes.” How is this best classified?
y: Something happened (an event), and the acetone is still acetone, now as a gas: a physical change.
No new substance formed; evaporation only changes the state.
A property describes what a substance is or can do; this note describes an event that happened.
A property is not an event, and evaporation does not form a new substance.
h: First decide: property (a description) or change (an event)? Then: did a new substance form?
w: The note describes an event, so it is a change, and evaporation forms no new substance, so it is a physical change. “Acetone evaporates easily” would be a physical property; “acetone is flammable” would be a chemical property.

q: A dental hygienist paints a liquid sealant onto a molar and shines a curing light on it. The light triggers a reaction that links the small molecules of the liquid into a hard, solid plastic that will not melt back into the original liquid. What kind of change is this?
c: Chemical, because new substances with different properties form
Physical, because the sealant only changed from liquid to solid
Physical, because light was the only thing added
Chemical, because every change from liquid to solid is chemical
y: The small molecules are joined into new, larger molecules, and the change cannot be reversed by warming, so new substances formed.
Freezing is physical, but here the molecules themselves were linked into new ones; it is not simple freezing.
Adding light does not make a change physical; what matters is whether new substances form.
Freezing water is liquid to solid and is physical, so this rule is not true.
h: Is the hardened sealant still the same substance as the liquid, just colder or in a new state?
w: The curing light starts a reaction that joins small molecules into a new, solid plastic that does not turn back into the liquid. New substances formed, so it is a chemical change, even though it looks like a liquid becoming a solid.

q: The diagram shows a sample before and after a change. What kind of change is shown?
c: Chemical: water molecules were broken down and new H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub> molecules formed
Physical: water changed from liquid to gas
Physical: the same molecules were only moved farther apart
y: The After box has new particles (H<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>) that were not in the Before box, so atoms were rearranged into new substances.
Water vapor would still be H<sub>2</sub>O molecules, but the After box has no H<sub>2</sub>O at all.
The particles after are different molecules, not the same molecules spread out.
Count the atoms: 8 H and 4 O before, 8 H and 4 O after. Atoms are rearranged, not destroyed.
h: Compare the kinds of particles in the two boxes. Are they the same molecules?
w: Before: 4 H2O. After: 4 H2 and 2 O2. The atoms (8 H and 4 O) are all still there but are rearranged into new substances, so this is a chemical change (the decomposition of water, which happens when an electric current is passed through it).

q: The diagram shows a sample before and after a change. Which statement best describes it?
c: A physical change: the particles are the same H<sub>2</sub>O molecules before and after
A chemical change: new molecules formed
A chemical change: the molecules lost some of their atoms
A physical change: the water became a new element
y: Every particle in both boxes is an H<sub>2</sub>O molecule, so the substance did not change identity.
No new kind of molecule appears in the After box.
Each molecule still has 2 H and 1 O in both boxes.
Water is a compound, and the particles after are still H<sub>2</sub>O, not a new element.
h: Look at what each particle is made of in both boxes.
w: Both boxes contain only H2O molecules. Whatever happened (melting, evaporating or just warming), the particles kept their identity, so it is a physical change. A particle diagram of a chemical change would show new kinds of particles after.

q: The diagram shows nitrogen and hydrogen before and after a reaction that makes ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, a fertilizer widely used on Valley farms. Which statement is correct?
c: The atoms are rearranged into new molecules, and the number of each kind of atom stays the same.
The atoms are rearranged, and some nitrogen atoms are destroyed.
No new substance forms, so this is a physical change.
New atoms are created to build the ammonia molecules.
y: Before: 4 N and 12 H atoms. After: 4 NH<sub>3</sub> also has 4 N and 12 H. New molecules, same atoms.
Count the N atoms: 4 before (in 2 N<sub>2</sub>) and 4 after (in 4 NH<sub>3</sub>). None are destroyed.
NH<sub>3</sub> is a new substance that was not present before, so this is a chemical change.
Atoms are never created in a chemical change; the 12 H atoms after were all there before.
h: Count each kind of atom in the Before box and in the After box.
w: Before: 2 N2 + 6 H2 = 4 N and 12 H atoms. After: 4 NH3 = 4 N and 12 H atoms. In a chemical change atoms are rearranged into new substances, but none are created or destroyed; this is why mass is conserved.

q: A 20.0 mL sample of an alcohol-based hand sanitizer has a mass of 17.4 g. What is its density?
y: d = m/V = 17.4 g ÷ 20.0 mL = 0.870 g/mL.
This is volume divided by mass (20.0 ÷ 17.4); the fraction is upside down.
This multiplies mass by volume; density divides mass by volume.
The number is right but the unit is inverted; mass ÷ volume gives g/mL.
h: Density = mass ÷ volume. Write the units in the fraction too.
w: d = m/V = 17.4 g ÷ 20.0 mL = 0.870 g/mL. Check: the mass in grams is less than the volume in mL, so the density should be less than 1 g/mL, and it is.

q: A medical lab technician measures a 10.0 mL urine sample and finds its mass is 10.2 g. What is the density of the sample?
y: d = 10.2 g ÷ 10.0 mL = 1.02 g/mL, slightly denser than pure water because of dissolved substances.
This is volume divided by mass (10.0 ÷ 10.2); density is mass divided by volume.
This multiplies mass by volume instead of dividing.
Check the decimal point: 10.2 ÷ 10.0 is a little more than 1, not about one-tenth.
h: The mass in grams is a little more than the volume in mL. Should the density be a little more or a little less than 1 g/mL?
w: d = m/V = 10.2 g ÷ 10.0 mL = 1.02 g/mL. Urine is a little denser than water (1.00 g/mL) because it carries dissolved salts and waste products.

q:
A small fishing weight has a mass of 56.5 g and a volume of 5.00 cm3. Using the densities given, which metal is it most likely made of?
aluminum 2.70 g/cm3; steel about 7.9 g/cm3; lead 11.3 g/cm3; gold 19.3 g/cm3
y: d = 56.5 g ÷ 5.00 cm<sup>3</sup> = 11.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, which matches lead.
Aluminum (2.70 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) is much less dense than the value you get from m/V here.
Steel (about 7.9 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) is less dense than this weight's calculated density.
Gold (19.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>) is denser than this weight's calculated density.
h: Calculate d = m/V, then find the matching density in the list.
w: d = m/V = 56.5 g ÷ 5.00 cm3 = 11.3 g/cm3, lead. Because density is intensive, it works as an identifying property no matter how big the sample is.

q: A geology student drops a piece of Sierra granite with a mass of 39.6 g into a graduated cylinder. The water level rises from 20.0 mL to 35.0 mL. What is the density of the granite?
y: The rock's volume is 35.0 − 20.0 = 15.0 mL, and 39.6 g ÷ 15.0 mL = 2.64 g/mL.
This divides by the final level, 35.0 mL, which includes the water as well as the rock.
This divides by the starting water level, 20.0 mL, which is the water, not the rock.
This divides the rock's volume by its mass; the fraction is upside down.
h: The rock's volume is the change in the water level, not either reading by itself.
w: The rock's volume is the water it displaces: 35.0 mL − 20.0 mL = 15.0 mL. Then d = 39.6 g ÷ 15.0 mL = 2.64 g/mL.

q: A plastic cap has a mass of 4.60 g and a volume of 5.00 mL. Water has a density of 1.00 g/mL and ethanol 0.789 g/mL. What happens to the cap in each liquid?
c: It floats in water and sinks in ethanol.
It sinks in water and floats in ethanol.
y: The cap's density is 4.60 ÷ 5.00 = 0.920 g/mL: less than water (floats) but more than ethanol (sinks).
This is reversed: an object floats only in a liquid denser than itself.
The cap is denser than ethanol, so it cannot float in ethanol.
The cap is less dense than water, so it floats in water.
h: Find the cap's density first, then compare it with each liquid's density.
w: d = 4.60 g ÷ 5.00 mL = 0.920 g/mL. It is less dense than water (1.00 g/mL), so it floats in water, and denser than ethanol (0.789 g/mL), so it sinks in ethanol.

q: Honey (1.42 g/mL), water (1.00 g/mL) and mineral oil (0.85 g/mL) are carefully poured into a tall cylinder and form three separate layers. What is the order of the layers from top to bottom?
y: The least dense liquid floats on top and the densest sinks to the bottom: 0.85, then 1.00, then 1.42 g/mL.
This is bottom to top; the densest liquid (honey) belongs at the bottom.
Water (1.00 g/mL) is denser than mineral oil (0.85 g/mL), so it cannot sit on top of the oil.
Honey is denser than water, so it sinks below the water rather than sitting above it.
h: Least dense on top, densest on the bottom.
w: Liquids that do not mix stack with the least dense on top: mineral oil (0.85), then water (1.00), then honey (1.42) on the bottom.

q: Ice has a density of 0.917 g/mL and liquid water 1.00 g/mL. Why does ice float on a lake?
c: Ice is less dense than liquid water.
Ice weighs less than the whole lake.
Ice is a solid, and all solids float on their liquids.
Ice is denser than liquid water.
y: An object floats in a liquid that is denser than it is, and 0.917 g/mL is less than 1.00 g/mL.
Floating depends on comparing densities, not on comparing total masses.
For most substances the solid is denser than the liquid and sinks; water is an exception.
If ice were denser than water, it would sink.
h: Compare the two densities given.
w: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water (0.917 g/mL versus 1.00 g/mL). Water is unusual: for most substances the solid is denser than the liquid and sinks. Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top down.

q: A 40.0 g block of paraffin wax has a density of 0.900 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. It is cut into two equal halves. What is the density of each half?
y: Cutting halves both the mass and the volume, so their ratio, the density, does not change.
This halves the density, but density is intensive; halving the mass also halves the volume.
Doubling the density would need more mass in the same volume; nothing was added.
20.0 is the mass of each half in grams, not its density.
h: Is density an intensive or an extensive property?
w: Each half has half the mass and half the volume, so d = m/V stays the same: 0.900 g/cm3. Density is an intensive property; it does not depend on the size of the sample.

q: Which statement best explains why a gas has a much lower density than a liquid or a solid?
c: Its particles are far apart, so very little mass is packed into each milliliter.
Its particles are larger than those in liquids and solids.
Its particles are packed more tightly than in liquids.
y: Density is mass per volume, and a gas is mostly empty space, so each milliliter holds very little mass.
Gas particles do have mass; a tank of oxygen weighs more when it is full than when it is empty.
Particle size is not what makes gases low in density; the space between particles is.
Gas particles are far apart, not packed tightly.
h: Density is mass per volume. Think about how much of a gas's volume is empty space.
w: Gas particles are far apart, so little mass is packed into each milliliter. Air, for example, is about 0.0012 g/mL, roughly a thousand times less dense than water.

q: A radiographer explains why the lungs appear dark on a chest X-ray while the ribs appear white. Air in the lungs has a density of about 0.0012 g/mL, and bone is much denser. Which statement fits?
c: X-rays pass easily through low-density air, so more reach the detector and the lungs look dark.
X-rays are absorbed most by the lowest-density materials, so the lungs look dark.
Air is denser than bone, so it blocks the X-rays.
Density has no effect on how X-rays pass through the body.
y: Low-density matter absorbs few X-rays, so more of them reach the detector there and the image is dark.
This is reversed: denser materials such as bone absorb more X-rays.
Air (about 0.0012 g/mL) is far less dense than bone.
Density is one of the main reasons different tissues appear different on an X-ray.
h: Which absorbs more X-rays: something with a lot of mass packed into each milliliter, or something mostly made of empty space?
w: Air in the lungs has a very low density, so X-rays pass through easily and the lungs look dark (radiolucent). Bone is denser and contains calcium, so it absorbs more X-rays and looks white (radiopaque).

q: Fresh milk from a Tulare County dairy is left standing in a jar, and a layer of cream rises to the top. What does this tell you about the cream?
c: The cream is less dense than the rest of the milk.
The cream is denser than the rest of the milk.
The cream has more mass than the rest of the milk.
The cream and the rest of the milk have the same density.
y: Less dense liquids rise and float above denser ones, so the cream must be less dense.
A denser layer would sink to the bottom, not rise to the top.
The layer order depends on density, not on total mass; the cream layer is actually the smaller amount.
If the densities were the same, the cream would have no reason to separate and rise.
h: In a density column, which layers end up on top?
w: The cream (rich in milkfat) rises because it is less dense than the watery part of the milk. Layers settle by density, with the least dense on top, just like oil on vinegar.

q: A red blood cell is about 0.0000075 m across. Which shows this length correctly in scientific notation?
y: The decimal point moves 6 places to the right to reach 7.5, and a number smaller than 1 gets a negative exponent.
A positive exponent describes a number larger than 1; this would be 7,500,000 m, far bigger than a cell.
Count the moves again: from 0.0000075 to 7.5 the decimal point passes six digits, not five.
75 × 10<sup>−7</sup> has the right value, but in scientific notation the coefficient must be at least 1 and less than 10.
h: Move the decimal point until one nonzero digit is in front of it, and count the moves.
w: Move the decimal point 6 places right: 0.0000075 → 7.5. A value less than 1 gets a negative exponent, so the length is 7.5 × 10−6 m. The coefficient (7.5) is between 1 and 10, as scientific notation requires.

q: A lab report lists a white blood cell count of 7.2 × 10<sup>3</sup> cells per microliter. Which is the same value as an ordinary number?
y: A positive exponent of 3 moves the decimal point 3 places to the right: 7.2 becomes 7200.
Moving the decimal point 4 places gives 72,000; the exponent 3 calls for only 3 moves.
This moves the decimal point only 2 places; the exponent 3 calls for 3.
A positive exponent makes the number larger than the coefficient, not smaller; this moved the decimal point the wrong way.
h: A positive exponent means a number bigger than the coefficient. Move the decimal point that many places.
w: 103 = 1000, so 7.2 × 1000 = 7200. Written this way, the two trailing zeros are not significant, which matches the two significant figures in 7.2.

q: Which unit is the SI base unit of mass?
y: The kilogram is the one SI base unit that already carries a prefix; every other mass unit is defined from it.
The gram is a common metric unit, but the SI chose the kilogram, not the gram, as its base unit of mass.
A milligram is a small metric unit derived from the gram; it is not a base unit.
The pound is a U.S. customary unit, not part of the SI.
h: One SI base unit is unusual because its name already includes a prefix.
w: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram. It is the only base unit whose name includes a prefix (kilo- = 1000), so 1 kg = 1000 g.

q: Which of these is not an SI base unit?
y: The liter is a derived unit of volume: it is defined from length (1 L is the volume of a cube 1 dm on each side).
The meter is the SI base unit of length.
The second is the SI base unit of time.
The kelvin is the SI base unit of temperature.
h: Base units cannot be built from other units. Which of these is really a length cubed?
w: Length (meter), time (second), mass (kilogram), temperature (kelvin) and amount of substance (mole) are SI base units. The liter is a derived unit of volume: 1 L = 1 dm3 = 1000 cm3.

q: The spores of the fungus that causes Valley fever (coccidioidomycosis) are only a few micrometers (µm) across. What does the prefix micro- (µ) mean?
y: Micro- means 10<sup>−6</sup>, so 1 µm = 10<sup>−6</sup> m and there are a million micrometers in a meter.
One-thousandth is milli- (m), as in millimeter; micro- is a thousand times smaller than milli-.
One-hundredth is centi- (c), as in centimeter.
One-billionth is nano- (n), as in nanometer; micro- is a thousand times larger than nano-.
h: Put the small prefixes in order: centi-, milli-, micro-, nano-. Each step after milli- is a factor of 1000.
w: Micro- (µ) = 10−6. The small prefixes go centi- (10−2), milli- (10−3), micro- (10−6), nano- (10−9). Clinical orders often write mcg for micrograms so the µ is not misread as m.

q: Which equality is correct?
y: Milli- means one-thousandth, so it takes 1000 milligrams to make one gram.
This is upside down: a milligram is much smaller than a gram, so one milligram cannot equal a thousand grams.
Kilo- means 1000, so 1 kg = 1000 g, not 100 g.
Centi- means one-hundredth, so 1 m = 100 cm, not 10 cm.
h: The larger unit gets the 1. How many of the smaller unit fit in it?
w: Milli- = 10−3, so 1 g = 1000 mg. A good habit: put the 1 in front of the larger unit and the big number in front of the smaller unit (1 kg = 1000 g, 1 m = 100 cm).

q: Four samples of flour are weighed for a food-science lab. Which sample has the largest mass?
y: 1 g = 100 cg, so 5.2 × 10<sup>4</sup> cg ÷ 100 = 520 g, the largest of the four.
0.50 kg is 500 g; it is large, but one of the other samples is 20 g more.
455 g is already in grams, and it is actually the smallest: the other three are 480 g, 500 g and 520 g once you convert them.
1 g = 1000 mg, so 4.8 × 10<sup>5</sup> mg is 480 g, which is not the largest.
h: Convert every mass to grams before you compare.
w: In grams: 0.50 kg = 500 g; 455 g; 4.8 × 105 mg = 480 g; 5.2 × 104 cg = 520 g. The largest is 5.2 × 104 cg. A big number in front of a small unit can still be a small amount, so always compare in the same unit.

q: A broth culture has 3.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> bacterial cells, and each cell has a mass of about 2.0 × 10<sup>−12</sup> g. What is the total mass of the cells?
y: Multiply the coefficients (3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0) and add the exponents (4 + (−12) = −8).
When you multiply powers of ten, you add the exponents; multiplying them (4 × −12) gives −48.
Subtracting the exponents (4 − (−12) = 16) is the rule for division, not multiplication.
The coefficients are multiplied, not added; 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 is the slip here.
h: Multiply the coefficients; add the exponents.
w: (3.0 × 104)(2.0 × 10−12 g) = (3.0 × 2.0) × 104 + (−12) g = 6.0 × 10−8 g. On the TI-36X Pro, enter each number with the ×10n key so the calculator keeps the powers of ten together.

q: A Valley water district delivers 8.4 × 10<sup>6</sup> L of water in one day to 2.1 × 10<sup>3</sup> homes. On average, how many liters is that per home?
y: Liters per home means liters ÷ homes: 8.4 ÷ 2.1 = 4.0, and 6 − 3 = 3 for the exponent.
This divides homes by liters, so the fraction is upside down; the answer must have liters on top.
When you divide powers of ten, you subtract the exponents; 6 + 3 = 9 adds them.
This multiplies the two numbers; "per home" means divide by the number of homes.
h: "Per home" means divide by the number of homes. When dividing, subtract the exponents.
w: (8.4 × 106 L) ÷ (2.1 × 103) = (8.4 ÷ 2.1) × 106 − 3 L = 4.0 × 103 L per home.

q: A virus particle is about 1 × 10<sup>−7</sup> m across. Which length is about the same?
y: 1 nm = 10<sup>−9</sup> m, so 10<sup>−7</sup> m ÷ 10<sup>−9</sup> m per nm = 10<sup>2</sup> = 100 nm.
10 nm is 10<sup>−8</sup> m, ten times smaller than the virus.
1 µm is 10<sup>−6</sup> m, ten times larger than the virus.
100 µm is 10<sup>−4</sup> m, about the width of a hair and a thousand times larger than the virus.
h: Write each choice as a power of ten in meters: nano- = 10<sup>−9</sup>, micro- = 10<sup>−6</sup>.
w: Nano- = 10−9, so 10−7 m = 102 × 10−9 m = 100 nm. Viruses are usually measured in nanometers; bacteria and cells in micrometers.

q: On a TI-36X Pro, which key sequence enters 3.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup>?
y: The ×10<sup>n</sup> key already supplies "times ten to the," so you type only the coefficient, the key, and the signed exponent.
Typing × 10 before the ×10<sup>n</sup> key multiplies by an extra 10, so the calculator holds 3.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup>.
Leaving out the negative sign enters 3.5 × 10<sup>4</sup>, a number 10<sup>8</sup> times too large.
The ^ key raises 3.5 itself to the −4 power, which is a completely different number.
h: The ×10<sup>n</sup> key stands for the whole "× 10 to the" part.
w: Type the coefficient, press ×10n, then the negative key (−) and 4. Use the (−) key for a negative exponent, not the subtraction key.

q: How many significant figures are in 0.004050 g?
y: Leading zeros (0.00) only place the decimal point; 4, 0, 5 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point all count.
This counts every digit, but the leading zeros before the 4 are placeholders and never count.
The zeros right after the decimal point (before the 4) are leading zeros, so they do not count.
The final zero comes after a nonzero digit and to the right of the decimal point, so it is significant.
h: Start counting at the first nonzero digit. Does the last zero count when there is a decimal point?
w: Start at the first nonzero digit: 4050. The zero between 4 and 5 is captive (always counts), and the trailing zero counts because the number has a decimal point. That makes 4 significant figures.

q: Which measurement has exactly two significant figures?
y: Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not significant, so only the 3 and 8 count.
The decimal point after the zeros makes them significant, so this has four significant figures.
In scientific notation every digit in the coefficient counts, so 3.80 has three significant figures.
Leading zeros do not count, but the trailing zeros after the decimal point do, so this has four.
h: Trailing zeros count only when the number shows a decimal point.
w: 3800 mL has two significant figures: with no decimal point, its trailing zeros are placeholders. To show more precision, write 3800. mL (four) or 3.80 × 103 mL (three).

q: Which value has an unlimited number of significant figures?
y: A count of whole objects is exact: there are exactly 24 tablets, not 23.9 or 24.1.
A volume read from glassware is a measurement, so it carries uncertainty and three significant figures.
A mass read from a scale is a measurement with uncertainty; it has two significant figures.
This equality is a rounded value (to four significant figures), so it is not exact, even though it is a conversion factor.
h: Exact numbers come from counting or from definitions. Which of these was counted?
w: Counted items are exact, so 24 tablets has unlimited significant figures and never limits a calculation. Defined equalities within one system (1 kg = 1000 g) and 1 in = 2.54 cm are exact too; rounded factors such as 1 lb = 453.6 g are not.

q: Round 0.0258449 to three significant figures.
y: The third significant digit is the 8, and the digit after it is 4, so the 8 stays.
This rounds in steps (449 → 45 → 5) instead of looking only at the first dropped digit, which is 4.
This keeps two significant figures, not three.
This keeps four significant figures (2, 5, 8, 4).
h: Find the third significant digit, then look only at the one digit right after it.
w: The significant digits start at 2: 2, 5, 8 | 449. The first dropped digit is 4 (less than 5), so the 8 stays: 0.0258. Never round in a chain of steps; look only at the first digit you drop.

q: One acetaminophen tablet has a mass of 0.325 g. What is the total mass of 12 tablets (counted)?
y: The count of 12 is exact, so the measured 0.325 g (three significant figures) sets the answer: 3.90 g.
This treats 12 as a measurement with two significant figures, but a count is exact and never limits the answer.
The calculator shows 3.9, and adding zeros claims four significant figures, more than 0.325 g supports.
This keeps only one significant figure, far less than the three in 0.325 g.
h: Counted numbers are exact. How many significant figures does the measured mass have?
w: 12 × 0.325 g = 3.9 on the calculator. The 12 is exact, so the answer keeps the three significant figures of 0.325 g: 3.90 g (the zero is added to show the third significant figure).

q: A pharmacy technician weighs a container (102 g, on a coarse scale), then adds 0.85 g and 1.236 g of two powders measured on an analytical balance. What is the total mass, to the correct precision?
y: In addition, the answer keeps the decimal places of the least precise value; 102 g is known only to the ones place.
This keeps every calculator digit; the total cannot be more precise than the 102 g measured to the ones place.
This keeps two decimal places, but 102 g has no decimal places, so the ones place is the limit.
This applies the multiplication rule (fewest significant figures); addition uses decimal places instead.
h: For addition and subtraction, look at decimal places, not the number of significant figures.
w: 102 + 0.85 + 1.236 = 104.086 g. The least precise value, 102 g, is known only to the ones place, so round to the ones place: 104 g.

q: A dental materials student finds the mass of a resin sample by difference (24.6 g − 22.1 g) and then divides by its volume, 1.335 mL. What density should she report?
y: The subtraction gives 2.5 g, which has only two significant figures, so the division result keeps two.
This keeps three significant figures, as if the mass still had three; after subtracting, 2.5 g has two.
This keeps four significant figures from the volume, ignoring the less precise mass.
This keeps only one significant figure; the mass (2.5 g) supports two.
h: Do the subtraction first and count the significant figures in that result before you divide.
w: Step 1 (subtraction, decimal-place rule): 24.6 g − 22.1 g = 2.5 g (tenths place, two significant figures). Step 2 (division): 2.5 g ÷ 1.335 mL = 1.8727… g/mL → two significant figures: 1.9 g/mL. Keep extra digits in the calculator between steps, but track the significant figures each step allows.

q: A microbiology student measures nutrient broth in the graduated cylinder shown. Each small mark is 0.5 mL. What volume should she record?
y: The marks are 0.5 mL apart, so you can be sure of the tenths place only by estimating it: about 16.3 mL.
This drops the estimated digit; a reading should go one place past what the marks show for certain.
With marks every 0.5 mL you cannot estimate to the hundredths place, so the last zero claims too much precision.
This reads the nearest line instead of estimating where the bottom of the meniscus sits between the lines.
h: Read the bottom of the meniscus. Record all certain digits plus one estimated digit.
w: The bottom of the meniscus sits a little past halfway between 16.0 and 16.5 mL. You are certain of 16, and you estimate the tenths: 16.3 mL (a nearby estimate such as 16.2 or 16.4 mL is also reasonable). The last digit is always the estimated one.

q: A biology student measures a pea seedling root with the ruler shown (marks every 0.1 cm). What length should she record?
y: The smallest marks are 0.1 cm apart, so you estimate one more digit, the hundredths: 3.47 cm.
This rounds away the estimated digit; with 0.1 cm marks you should report to the hundredths place.
The ruler cannot be read to the thousandths place, so the final zero is not justified.
This cuts off the reading at the last full mark instead of estimating how far past it the root reaches.
h: Count the certain digits from the marks, then estimate one more between the marks.
w: The end of the root is between the 3.4 and 3.5 cm marks, about seven-tenths of the way. Certain digits: 3.4; estimated digit: 7. Record 3.47 cm (3.46 or 3.48 cm would also be a fair estimate).

q: During a titration, a student reads the buret shown. The marks are 0.1 mL apart, and buret numbers increase going down. What is the reading?
y: Below the 13 mL label, the meniscus bottom sits between 13.6 and 13.7, about two-tenths of the way: 13.62 mL.
This reads the scale as if the numbers increase upward; on a buret, values grow as you go down.
This drops the estimated digit; with 0.1 mL marks a buret reading goes to the hundredths place.
A buret with 0.1 mL marks can be estimated only to the hundredths place, so the extra zero claims too much.
h: On a buret, 0.00 mL is at the top. Read the bottom of the meniscus and estimate the hundredths.
w: The meniscus bottom is just below the 13.6 mL mark (numbers increase downward). Certain: 13.6; estimated: 2. Record 13.62 mL. Buret readings always have two decimal places.

q: A student throws five darts at the target shown. Which description fits the throws?
y: The darts are close to each other (precise) but all land well away from the bullseye (not accurate).
Accurate means close to the true value (the bullseye); these darts are grouped far from it.
Not precise would mean scattered darts; these are tightly grouped.
Tightly grouped darts are precise even when they miss the bullseye.
h: Precision: are the darts close to each other? Accuracy: are they close to the bullseye?
w: The darts are tightly grouped, so the throws are precise, but the group is off to one side, so they are not accurate. In the lab this pattern usually points to a systematic error, such as a balance that needs calibrating.

q:
Four students each weigh the same 5.00 g reference mass three times.
Student A: 4.71 g, 4.72 g, 4.70 g
Student B: 5.01 g, 4.99 g, 5.00 g
Student C: 4.80 g, 5.25 g, 4.95 g
Student D: 4.55 g, 5.30 g, 4.70 g
Whose results are precise but not accurate?
y: A's readings agree within 0.02 g (precise), but they average 4.71 g, well below the true 5.00 g (not accurate).
B's readings agree closely and average 5.00 g, so they are both precise and accurate.
C's readings spread over 0.45 g, so they are not precise, even though their average is close to 5.00 g.
D's readings are widely scattered and average 4.85 g, so they are neither precise nor accurate.
h: For each student, check how close the three readings are to each other, then how close their average is to 5.00 g.
w: Student A: the readings span only 0.02 g (precise) but average 4.71 g, about 0.29 g low (not accurate). B is accurate and precise; C averages 5.00 g but is scattered (accurate on average, not precise); D is neither.

q: To convert 2.50 L to milliliters, which conversion factor should you multiply by?
y: Liters is on the bottom so it cancels with the L you start with, leaving mL on top.
With liters on top, the units would become L<sup>2</sup>/mL instead of canceling.
This factor is false: a milliliter is smaller than a liter, so 1 mL cannot equal 1000 L.
1 L is 1000 mL, not 100 mL; 100 would fit centi-, not milli-.
h: Put the unit you want to cancel on the bottom of the factor.
w: 2.50 L × (1000 mL / 1 L) = 2.50 × 103 mL. The starting unit goes on the bottom of the factor so it cancels, and the unit you want goes on top.

q: A newborn measures 19.5 in long. What is the length in centimeters? (1 in = 2.54 cm exactly)
y: 19.5 in × 2.54 cm/in = 49.53 cm; the exact factor does not limit the answer, so the three significant figures of 19.5 in give 49.5 cm.
This divides by 2.54; a centimeter is smaller than an inch, so the number of centimeters must be larger.
This keeps the calculator digits; the measured 19.5 in has only three significant figures.
This rounds to two significant figures, but the exact factor does not limit the answer; 19.5 in has three.
h: An inch is longer than a centimeter, so expect a bigger number. Is 2.54 exact?
w: 19.5 in × (2.54 cm / 1 in) = 49.53 cm → 49.5 cm. The factor 1 in = 2.54 cm is exact by definition, so only the measured 19.5 in (three significant figures) limits the answer.

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An order calls for 15.0 mg/kg of a medication. The child weighs 44.0 lb. Using 1 kg = 2.205 lb, what dose in milligrams does the order describe?
y: 44.0 lb ÷ 2.205 lb/kg = 19.95 kg, and 19.95 kg × 15.0 mg/kg = 299 mg (three significant figures).
This multiplies the weight in pounds by 15.0 mg/kg; the order is per kilogram, so convert pounds to kilograms first.
This multiplies by 2.205 instead of dividing, which makes the weight in kilograms larger than in pounds, the wrong direction.
The arithmetic is right, but every given value has three or four significant figures, so the answer keeps three.
h: First convert pounds to kilograms (a kilogram is heavier than a pound, so the number should shrink). Then multiply by mg/kg.
w: 44.0 lb × (1 kg / 2.205 lb) = 19.95 kg; 19.95 kg × (15.0 mg / 1 kg) = 299.3 mg → 299 mg. Check: the child is about 20 kg, and 20 × 15 = 300, so the answer is reasonable.

q: A vitamin B<sub>12</sub> tablet contains 2.50 × 10<sup>2</sup> µg of the vitamin. What is that mass in grams?
y: 1 g = 10<sup>6</sup> µg, so divide by 10<sup>6</sup>: 2.50 × 10<sup>2</sup> × 10<sup>−6</sup> = 2.50 × 10<sup>−4</sup> g.
This uses 1 g = 1000 µg, which is the factor for milligrams, not micrograms.
This multiplies by 10<sup>6</sup>; converting to a larger unit (grams) must give a smaller number.
This uses 10<sup>9</sup> per gram, the factor for nanograms, not micrograms.
h: Micro- = 10<sup>−6</sup>. Going to a bigger unit makes the number smaller.
w: 2.50 × 102 µg × (1 g / 106 µg) = 2.50 × 10−4 g. (That is 0.250 mg; orders write mcg for micrograms.)

q: Math practice only; always follow the order and facility policy. An IV infusion runs at 125 mL/h for a full 12-hour shift. How many liters are delivered?
y: 125 mL/h × 12 h = 1500 mL = 1.50 L; the shift length is a defined (exact) number, so the rate's three significant figures set the answer.
This treats the 12-hour shift as a measured value with two significant figures; the defined length of a shift is exact here.
This is the number of milliliters labeled as liters; 1500 mL must be divided by 1000 to give liters.
This divides the rate by the time; volume delivered is rate × time.
h: Rate × time gives volume. Then change mL to L.
w: 125 mL/h × 12 h = 1500 mL; 1500 mL × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 1.50 L. The hours cancel, and the 12 h shift is exact, so the answer keeps the three significant figures of 125 mL/h.

q: A wound care nurse records a skin wound area of 6.0 cm<sup>2</sup>. What is the area in mm<sup>2</sup>? (1 cm = 10 mm)
y: For squared units the factor is squared too: (10 mm/1 cm)<sup>2</sup> = 100 mm<sup>2</sup>/cm<sup>2</sup>, so 6.0 × 100 = 600 mm<sup>2</sup>.
This uses 10 mm/cm only once; an area unit is squared, so the factor must be squared too.
This divides by 100; a millimeter is smaller than a centimeter, so the number of mm<sup>2</sup> must be larger.
This cubes the factor (10<sup>3</sup>), which is right for volume, not for area.
h: 1 cm<sup>2</sup> is a square 10 mm on a side. How many mm<sup>2</sup> is that?
w: 6.0 cm2 × (10 mm / 1 cm)2 = 6.0 cm2 × 100 mm2/cm2 = 6.0 × 102 mm2. Scientific notation keeps the two significant figures clear.

q: A dairy's water storage tank holds 2.40 m<sup>3</sup>. How many liters is that? (1 m = 100 cm; 1 mL = 1 cm<sup>3</sup>)
y: (100 cm/m)<sup>3</sup> = 10<sup>6</sup> cm<sup>3</sup> per m<sup>3</sup>, which is 10<sup>6</sup> mL or 10<sup>3</sup> L, so 2.40 m<sup>3</sup> = 2.40 × 10<sup>3</sup> L.
This uses the 100 cm/m factor only once; a cubic unit needs the factor cubed.
This stops at cubic centimeters (2.40 × 10<sup>6</sup> cm<sup>3</sup>) and calls them liters; a cubic centimeter is a milliliter.
This divides where it should multiply; a cubic meter is much larger than a liter, so there are many liters in it.
h: Cube the length factor: (100 cm / 1 m)<sup>3</sup>. Then use 1 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1 mL.
w: 2.40 m3 × (100 cm / 1 m)3 = 2.40 × 106 cm3 = 2.40 × 106 mL; × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 2.40 × 103 L. (1 m3 = 1000 L.)

q: A microbiology prep room needs 25.0 g of ethanol (density 0.789 g/mL). What volume should be measured?
y: Use density as a conversion factor with grams on the bottom: 25.0 g × (1 mL / 0.789 g) = 31.7 mL.
This multiplies grams by g/mL, which leaves g<sup>2</sup>/mL; the grams must cancel.
This divides the density by the mass; the units would be 1/mL, not mL.
The setup is right, but 25.0 g and 0.789 g/mL each have three significant figures, so the answer keeps three.
h: Flip the density so grams are on the bottom: 1 mL / 0.789 g.
w: 25.0 g × (1 mL / 0.789 g) = 31.69 mL → 31.7 mL. Check: ethanol is less dense than water, so 25.0 g takes up more than 25.0 mL.

q: A unit of donated whole blood has a volume of 475 mL. Blood has a density of about 1.06 g/mL. What is the mass of the unit?
y: Volume × density: 475 mL × 1.06 g/mL = 503.5 g, which rounds to three significant figures as 504 g.
This divides the volume by the density; mL ÷ (g/mL) gives mL<sup>2</sup>/g, not grams.
This keeps the calculator digits; both given values have three significant figures.
This divides the density by the volume, which gives a tiny number with the wrong units.
h: Set up the units so mL cancels: mL × g/mL.
w: 475 mL × (1.06 g / 1 mL) = 503.5 g → 504 g. Check: blood is a little denser than water, so the mass in grams is a little more than the volume in mL.

q: A Valley olive mill fills a 2.00 L bottle with olive oil (density 0.917 g/mL). What is the mass of the oil in kilograms?
y: 2.00 L → 2000 mL; × 0.917 g/mL = 1834 g; ÷ 1000 g/kg = 1.83 kg (three significant figures).
This stops at grams (1834 g) but labels the result kilograms; one more step, g → kg, is needed.
This divides by the density instead of multiplying, so the units cannot come out as mass.
The steps are right, but every given value has three significant figures, so the answer keeps three.
h: Chain it: L → mL → g (density) → kg.
w: 2.00 L × (1000 mL / 1 L) × (0.917 g / 1 mL) × (1 kg / 1000 g) = 1.834 kg → 1.83 kg. Check: oil floats on water, so 2 L of oil should weigh a little less than 2 kg.

q: A bag of Valley almonds weighs 2.50 lb. Using 1 lb = 453.6 g, what is its mass in kilograms?
y: 2.50 lb × 453.6 g/lb = 1134 g; × 1 kg/1000 g = 1.134 kg, which rounds to three significant figures as 1.13 kg.
This is the mass in grams (1134 g) labeled as kilograms; the g → kg step was skipped.
This multiplies by 2.205 (lb per kg); a kilogram is heavier than a pound, so the number of kilograms must be smaller.
The setup is right, but 2.50 lb has three significant figures, so the answer keeps three.
h: Two steps: lb → g, then g → kg. A kilogram is heavier than a pound.
w: 2.50 lb × (453.6 g / 1 lb) × (1 kg / 1000 g) = 1.134 kg → 1.13 kg. The 453.6 g factor has four significant figures, so the measured 2.50 lb (three) limits the answer.
